prompt: The bank still runs on a decades-old system because too much depends on it to switch.
tells: too much depends on it to switch
why: An early choice now has so much built around it that changing is too costly. That's a locked-in choice.
trap: It may work fine; the point is that leaving it is too hard.

prompt: Keyboards still use a layout designed for old typewriters, because everyone has learned it.
why: Once millions learned the layout, changing it got harder every year. A choice that stuck because so much grew around it is lock-in.
trap: The layout doesn't enforce a rule; its history keeps it in place.

prompt: The company is stuck with an old file format because thousands of templates and scripts depend on it.
tells: thousands of templates and scripts depend on it
why: Everything built on the format makes switching expensive. That's a locked-in choice.
trap: The format isn't a gate everything passes through; it's hard to leave.

prompt: The railway keeps its narrow track width because changing it would mean rebuilding every line and train.
tells: would mean rebuilding every line and train
why: An early decision became costly to reverse once everything was built to fit it. That's lock-in.
trap: The tracks don't shape people's routines here; the issue is how hard the choice is to undo.

prompt: Moving off the cloud provider would mean redoing everything the team has built in five years.
why: Years of work built on one provider make leaving very costly. A choice that's hard to reverse is locked in.
trap: The provider isn't blocking a goal today; the trouble is leaving it.

prompt: The company keeps its old department structure because budgets, systems and job titles were all built around it.
tells: budgets, systems and job titles were all built around it
why: So much now depends on the old structure that changing it is hard. That's a locked-in choice.
trap: Nothing is changing back and forth; it's stuck because of what was built around it.
